title: MERGE — Insert, Update, Delete in One Statement
description: Use MERGE to synchronize a target table with a source table in a single atomic operation — insert new, update changed, and delete missing rows.

data.text: Imagine you receive a daily feed of product data, and you need to update your live table: add new products, change prices for existing ones, and remove discontinued items. Doing this with separate INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements is error-prone and slow. The MERGE statement does all three in one atomic pass.

data.title: Full MERGE structure
data.code:
MERGE target_table AS t
USING source_table AS s
ON t.key_col = s.key_col
WHEN MATCHED
    THEN UPDATE SET t.col1 = s.col1, t.col2 = s.col2
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET
    THEN INSERT (key_col, col1, col2) VALUES (s.key_col, s.col1, s.col2)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE
    THEN DELETE;

rows: Row exists in both target and source

data.title: Synchronize target with staging data
data.code:
MERGE sales.category AS t
USING  sales.category_staging AS s
ON     t.category_id = s.category_id
WHEN MATCHED
    THEN UPDATE SET
        t.category_name = s.category_name,
        t.amount        = s.amount
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET
    THEN INSERT (category_id, category_name, amount)
         VALUES (s.category_id, s.category_name, s.amount)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE
    THEN DELETE;

data.title: How the example syncs data
data.text: Rows 1, 3, 4 (in both tables) → UPDATE their amounts. Rows 5, 6 (source only) → INSERT. Row 2 (target only) → DELETE. The target table now matches the source exactly.
'Upsert' means 'insert or update' — if the row exists, update it; if not, insert it. This is one of the most common MERGE patterns:

data.title: Upsert — insert or update
data.code:
MERGE sales.inventory AS t
USING  sales.inventory_updates AS s
ON     t.product_id = s.product_id
WHEN MATCHED
    THEN UPDATE SET t.stock_level = s.stock_level, t.last_updated = GETDATE()
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET
    THEN INSERT (product_id, stock_level, last_updated)
         VALUES (s.product_id, s.stock_level, GETDATE());

items: The source table's join key must be unique, or MERGE raises an error — deduplicate your source data first
Always include a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE ... THEN DELETE if you want to remove missing rows; omit it if deletions are not desired
Test with a SELECT first to verify which rows match your ON condition
Wrap MERGE in a transaction if you need atomicity

data.title: Beware of the 'not matched' gotcha
data.text: If your source produces duplicate keys, SQL Server raises 'the source contains rows that match target...'. Always ensure the source has a unique key — use SELECT DISTINCT or GROUP BY if necessary.

data.title: MERGE essentials
points: MERGE synchronizes a target table with a source in one atomic operation
WHEN MATCHED → UPDATE; WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET → INSERT; WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE → DELETE
The source join key must be unique — deduplicate if needed
Upsert (insert-or-update) is the most common MERGE pattern
Always test the ON matching condition with a SELECT before running MERGE

data.text: For simpler upserts, SQL Server 2008+ also supports the OUTPUT clause with INSERT. And as of SQL Server 2022, the new 'INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY' style is emerging. But MERGE remains the standard approach for full synchronization across most supported versions.
